lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Advanced welding is not just about joining metal; it is about creating strong, safe, and lasting structures that can withstand the demands of African industry, construction, and repair work. Whether you are welding a trailer chassis in Nairobi, repairing a water tank in Lagos, or building a gate in Accra, the quality of your weld determines safety and durability. Basic welding gets two pieces stuck together. Advanced welding ensures the joint can carry loads, resist vibration, and survive years of exposure to sun, rain, and dust. In many African markets, skilled welders who can work with different metals and positions earn 2-3 times more than general welders. For example, a certified welder on a pipeline project in Tanzania can earn $30-$50 per day, while an unskilled welder might earn $5-$10. This module takes you beyond simple flat-position stick welding. You will learn to select the right process for the job, prepare metal properly, control heat, and troubleshoot defects. You will also learn safety practices that prevent injury and death. Welding is dangerous: electric shock, fumes, burns, and eye damage are real risks. But with the right techniques and gear, you can work safely and productively. By the end of this module, you will be able to make high-quality welds in various positions, identify and fix common defects, and apply best practices on any job site. This knowledge is your ticket to better pay and more respect in the trade. Letâs get started.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To do advanced welding, you need more than a basic arc welder and a chipping hammer. Start with a reliable welding machine. For stick welding (SMAW), a 200-amp inverter welder works well on 220V single-phase, common in many African workshops. For MIG welding, a 200-amp MIG with gas capability is ideal. You will also need an angle grinder with 115mm or 230mm discs for cutting and grinding. A wire brush, chipping hammer, and slag hammer are essential for cleaning welds. For measuring and marking, get a steel tape, combination square, and soapstone or marker. Clamps (C-clamps, magnetic clamps) hold parts in place. Personal protective equipment (PPE) is non-negotiable: auto-darkening welding helmet with at least shade 10-13, leather gloves, flame-resistant jacket, safety boots, and a respirator for fumes. For materials, mild steel is the most common and easiest to weld. You will also encounter stainless steel (needs different electrodes and lower heat) and aluminum (requires AC TIG or spool gun MIG). Electrodes: for mild steel, use E6013 for general work and E7018 for high-strength joints. For stainless, use 308L or 316L rods. Filler wire for MIG: ER70S-6 for mild steel. Shielding gas: for MIG, use 75% argon/25% CO2 mix for steel; for TIG, pure argon. Always store electrodes in a dry place; moisture causes porosity. In Africa, you can find these tools at hardware stores in major cities or order online. Invest in quality; cheap tools cost more in downtime and bad welds.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps for a strong advanced weld. First, prepare the metal. Clean it with a grinder to bare shiny metal, removing rust, paint, and oil. Bevel edges for thick metal (over 6mm) to ensure penetration. Set your machine: for 3.2mm E6013 electrode on mild steel, set around 90-120 amps. For 4.0mm, use 120-160 amps. For MIG on 6mm steel, set voltage to 20-22V and wire speed to 4-5 m/min. Clamp your work securely. Second, tack weld the pieces at both ends and middle to prevent distortion. Third, start welding. For stick, strike the arc like a match, then maintain a short arc (arc length about equal to electrode diameter). Use a drag angle of 10-15 degrees. For a flat butt weld, move in a straight line or slight weave. For vertical up, use a triangle or Z weave, pausing at edges. For overhead, use lower amperage and faster travel. Fourth, control heat input. If the metal gets too hot (turns blue or grey), stop and let it cool. Overheating causes warping and weakens the weld. Fifth, after welding, clean the slag with a chipping hammer and wire brush. Inspect for defects: cracks, porosity, undercut. If you find a defect, grind it out and re-weld. Finally, let the weld cool naturally; do not quench with water unless specified, as rapid cooling can cause cracking. Practice each position on scrap metal before doing a real job. Remember, consistency in travel speed, angle, and arc length is key.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Even experienced welders make mistakes. Here are common ones and how to fix them. 1) Porosity: small holes in the weld caused by moisture, oil, or too long an arc. Fix: clean metal, use dry electrodes, and shorten arc. 2) Undercut: a groove melted into the base metal along the weld toe. Caused by too high amperage or wrong angle. Fix: reduce amps, adjust angle to 10-15 degrees, and use a slight weave. 3) Slag inclusion: trapped slag inside the weld. Happens when you don't clean between passes or use wrong polarity. Fix: clean thoroughly, use correct polarity (electrode positive for E6013). 4) Spatter: small metal droplets stuck to the workpiece. Caused by too high amperage or long arc. Fix: reduce amps, shorten arc, use anti-spatter spray. 5) Warping: metal bends due to uneven heating. Fix: clamp securely, use tack welds, alternate welding sides, and allow cooling. 6) Incomplete penetration: weld doesn't reach the root. Fix: increase root gap, higher amps, slower travel. 7) Cracking: often from rapid cooling or high carbon steel. Fix: preheat thick steel, use low-hydrogen electrodes like E7018, and cool slowly. 8) Wrong electrode angle: leads to uneven beads. Fix: maintain 10-15 degree drag angle. Always inspect your work with a flashlight and magnifying glass. If you find a defect, grind it out completely and re-weld. Never try to cover up a defect with another pass; it will fail. Practice on scrap until you can consistently produce clean welds.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Welding safety is not optional; it saves lives. In Africa, many workshops lack proper ventilation, so you must protect yourself. Always wear an auto-darkening helmet with correct shade: shade 10 for low amps, 13 for high amps. Never look at the arc without protection; it causes arc eye (painful burns to the cornea). Wear leather gloves, a flame-resistant long-sleeve jacket, and safety boots. Use a respirator when welding galvanized or painted metal, as fumes are toxic. Ensure good ventilation: open doors and windows, use a fan to blow fumes away, but not directly on the weld (it disrupts shielding gas). Keep a fire extinguisher nearby and a bucket of sand or water. Never weld near flammable materials. Check your cables for damage; exposed wires cause electric shock. Ground the work clamp securely. Work on a dry surface, not wet ground. When welding overhead, wear a cap and ear plugs to keep sparks out. Keep your work area clean and organized. Store gas cylinders upright and secured. Never weld a closed container; it can explode. Best practices: plan your weld, use the right process for the metal, and don't rush. Take breaks to avoid fatigue. Stay hydrated. If you feel dizzy, stop and get fresh air. Finally, get trained in first aid for burns and electric shock. Your safety is your responsibility.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to practice. This exercise will help you apply what you've learned. You will need: mild steel plates (100mm x 100mm x 6mm), a stick welder (200A), E6013 electrodes (3.2mm), angle grinder, wire brush, chipping hammer, clamps, and PPE. Task 1: Butt weld in flat position. Clean two plates, bevel edges if needed, tack weld at both ends. Set amperage to 100-120A. Weld a straight bead along the joint. Clean slag, inspect for porosity and undercut. Task 2: T-joint in horizontal position. Place one plate vertical on another, tack weld. Weld along the joint using a slight weave. Use 110-130A. Task 3: Vertical up weld. Set two plates vertically with a gap, tack. Weld from bottom to top using a triangle weave, pausing at edges. Use 90-110A. Task 4: Overhead weld. Position plates overhead (secure safely). Use 80-100A, short arc, fast travel. After each task, grind out any defects and re-weld. Record your settings and observations. Aim for consistent bead width and penetration. If you don't have a welder, visit a local workshop and ask to practice under supervision. Alternatively, use a welding simulator app. After completing, compare your welds to the examples in the module. Take photos and share with your instructor or peers for feedback. Repeat until you can produce clean, strong welds in all positions. This practice is the foundation for advanced certification.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between basic and advanced welding?
options: A) Advanced welding uses only MIG
B) Advanced welding focuses on strength, safety, and versatility
C) Basic welding is only for thin metal
D) Advanced welding requires no safety gear
quiz.explanation: Advanced welding ensures joints can carry loads and last, while basic welding just sticks metal together.

quiz.q: Which electrode is commonly used for general mild steel welding?
quiz.explanation: E6013 is a general-purpose electrode for mild steel.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade for a welding helmet when using high amperage?
quiz.explanation: Shade 13 protects eyes from bright arc at high amps.

quiz.q: What causes porosity in a weld?
options: B) Moisture or oil on metal
quiz.explanation: Porosity is caused by contaminants like moisture or oil.

quiz.q: How should you fix undercut?
options: B) Reduce amperage and adjust angle
C) Weld over it without cleaning
quiz.explanation: Undercut is fixed by reducing heat and correcting electrode angle.

quiz.q: What is the correct polarity for E6013 electrode?
quiz.explanation: E6013 typically uses electrode positive (DCEP) for good penetration.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding thick metal?
quiz.explanation: Beveling ensures proper penetration on thick metal.

quiz.q: What is a tack weld?
options: A) A small weld to hold parts in place
quiz.explanation: Tack welds temporarily hold parts aligned before full welding.

quiz.q: Which gas mixture is common for MIG welding of steel?
quiz.explanation: 75/25 argon/CO2 provides good penetration and arc stability.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of welding galvanized metal?
quiz.explanation: Galvanized coating releases toxic zinc fumes when welded.

quiz.q: What should you do if you get arc eye?
quiz.explanation: Arc eye is a corneal burn and requires medical attention.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a wire brush in welding?
options: A) To clean slag and dirt
quiz.explanation: Wire brush removes slag and contaminants between passes.

quiz.q: What causes spatter?
options: B) Too high amperage or long arc
quiz.explanation: High amperage or long arc causes molten metal to splatter.

quiz.q: How can you prevent warping?
options: B) Clamp and use tack welds
quiz.explanation: Clamping and tacking reduce heat distortion.

quiz.q: What is incomplete penetration?
options: B) Weld doesn't reach the root
D) Weld has too much spatter
quiz.explanation: Incomplete penetration means the weld metal did not fuse at the root.

quiz.q: Which electrode is low-hydrogen?
quiz.explanation: E7018 is a low-hydrogen electrode, reducing cracking risk.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding a closed container?
quiz.explanation: Closed containers can explode due to trapped gases.

quiz.q: What is the correct travel angle for stick welding?
quiz.explanation: A 10-15 degree drag angle gives good penetration and bead shape.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the step-by-step method?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning metal to bare shiny surface is essential before welding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended amperage for 3.2mm E6013 electrode?
quiz.explanation: 90-120A is typical for 3.2mm E6013 on mild steel.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a respirator in welding?
quiz.explanation: Respirator prevents inhalation of toxic welding fumes.

quiz.q: What is slag inclusion?
quiz.explanation: Slag inclusion is non-metallic solid material trapped in the weld.

quiz.q: How should you store electrodes?
quiz.explanation: Moisture causes porosity, so store electrodes dry.

quiz.q: What is the main danger of electric shock in welding?
quiz.explanation: Electric shock can be fatal; always check cables and ground.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to cool a weld?
quiz.explanation: Natural cooling prevents cracking; quenching can cause hardening.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of cracking?
quiz.explanation: Rapid cooling can cause thermal stresses leading to cracks.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a chipping hammer?
quiz.explanation: Chipping hammer removes slag after welding.

quiz.q: Which position is most difficult for beginners?
quiz.explanation: Overhead welding is challenging due to gravity and molten metal falling.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a defect in your weld?
options: A) Cover it with another pass
B) Grind it out and re-weld
quiz.explanation: Defects must be completely removed and re-welded for strength.

quiz.q: What is the recommended voltage for MIG welding 6mm steel?
quiz.explanation: 20-22V is typical for MIG on 6mm steel with ER70S-6 wire.
